workItems.title: Requirement coverage: approved exceptions
acceptance: A requirement may be accepted without proof only through a recorded exception carrying owner, reason, risk and an expiry date
An expired exception fails the gate rather than ageing into silence
The exception record is machine-readable and counted in the same coverage report as proven requirements
workItems.notes:
Narrowed by the D-013 audit from the original row (every accepted requirement points to proof OR an approved exception). The coverage half is done: readiness.js requires requirements-traceability at R2, docs-lint enforces the intent/spec/task chain, DV-002 extended it upstream to pain points, and all three reference apps ship docs/requirements-traceability.md. The exception half does not exist at all — there is no waiver record anywhere in the repository, and readiness.js only offers not-applicable, which is restricted to four conditional controls and means something different (the capability is absent, not that the risk was accepted). Without it the only way to ship a known, accepted gap is to lie in the manifest or to not record it, which is the failure mode the whole evidence model exists to prevent.

Work done 2026-09-23. The artifact is docs/evidence/requirement-coverage.json (requirement-coverage 1.0): every accepted requirement answers with exactly one of proof or an exception, and having both is an error because one of the two is then untrue. The decisive design choice was refusing manual-only proof. Without it the whole mechanism is bypassable by typing "checked by hand", and the repository already contained the case that proves it: nextjs-postgres-crud's traceability table claimed the audit trail was verified against a live database during PP-003, which is evidence living in a session that no longer exists. It is now REQ-004, an accepted risk expiring 2026-12-22, and react-fastapi-postgres-crud proves the same requirement with a real test, so the honest reading is a missing test in one app rather than a design flaw.

The corpus is not invented: all 12 exceptions across the three apps come from the "Known limitations (not fixed — documented instead of hidden)" sections already written in docs/security-notes.md, plus that one traceability row. Those sections were honest and machine-invisible at the same time, which is a third failure mode next to lying in a manifest and not recording the gap at all. One item was deliberately NOT converted: expo's Math.random local ids, whose own note argues no requirement goes unmet because ids are never capability tokens; recording it would inflate the pile of accepted risk, which is the disease D-013 and D-014 had just treated.

Expiry is deliberately the opposite call from EP-010. There the window is the verifier's because evidence that declares its own freshness declares itself fresh forever, and the outcome is EXPIRED, which is nobody's fault. Here expiresOn belongs to the person who signed for the risk, so passing it is a promise that was not kept and the outcome is FAIL. The 2099 loophole is closed the same way EP-010 closed its own: --max-window-days is supplied by the verifier, unset means reported not judged, and npm run check supplies 90 days for the reference apps, the same number evidence-freshness.yml already uses. gate.js deliberately supplies none, because how much risk may be pre-accepted is the adopting project's appetite, not the kit's.

Additive throughout, which is why 3.1.0 is MINOR: a project with no requirement-coverage.json is not checked, and no gate that passed before fails now. readiness.js changed only by exporting validateEvidence so both artifacts share one definition of what counts as evidence — two definitions drifting apart is contract-drift, a named class in EV-003's taxonomy.

Named requirement-coverage.js rather than coverage.js after finding the collision: .claude/run.js already has a coverage subcommand meaning test coverage, and the CLI command is buaflow requirements for the same reason.

Proven beyond the suite: backdating one exception to 2026-06-01 turns npm run check red and names the control, and restoring it turns it green. Suite 250/250 (was 233), 45 work items, 35 done.

workItems.title: Security baseline: ASVS mapping and threat boundaries
acceptance: A named external control set is mapped to concrete project evidence rather than to a checklist invented here
Threat boundaries are recorded as an artifact a reviewer can check, not only described in prose
The security-controls control cites that mapping instead of free text
workItems.notes:
Narrowed by the D-013 audit. The scanning half is done and enforced: secrets-scan, dependency-scan and security-controls are required at R3, gate.js refuses to downgrade the scanner modes in production assurance, and all three apps ship gitleaks and dependency-audit evidence. The mapping half does not exist. ASVS appears in exactly two files — the roadmap and standards/deployment-ready-contract.md, where the security-controls row asks for "threat boundary + applicable ASVS/control proof" — and nothing produces or checks such a mapping, so today that control is satisfied by prose in docs/security-notes.md. The roadmap cites ASVS as a research baseline precisely so the checklist is not invented here, and that intent is currently unimplemented.

Work done 2026-09-23. The control set is a pinned copy, not a checklist: standards/control-sets/owasp-asvs-5.0.0-l1.json holds the 70 Level 1 requirements of OWASP ASVS 5.0.0, extracted from the published English sources at tag v5.0.0, with the sha256 of each upstream chapter file recorded so the copy is traceable rather than trusted. That matters because standards/security-checklist.md is a checklist this repository wrote for itself, and a project that grades itself against its own list is the same problem as a north-star metric whose denominator is its own reference apps; that file now says so explicitly and points here for standards claims. The version was checked rather than remembered — ASVS 5.0 restructured the chapters completely from 4.0, has no Level 1 requirements at all in V16 and exactly one in V13, and inventing those numbers from memory would have been the same defect in a new disguise.

Three rules carry the artifact. Threat boundaries are data, not a paragraph: each names the untrusted side, the trusted side, the assets, the entry-point files and the files that enforce the rule, and those files must exist, because a boundary pointing at deleted code describes a system that is gone. Every control of a non-excluded chapter must be answered, so a baseline cannot be a list of the controls that happened to pass; a whole chapter can be excluded once with a reason, which is what keeps it from becoming seventy identical not-applicable rows. And not-met must cite an approved exception that really exists in the same project's requirement-coverage.json, which is the link back to EP-002: an accepted risk has exactly one home, it expires under the same rule, and citing a proven requirement instead is refused so a passing requirement cannot launder a failing control. That cross-artifact check earned its keep on its first run by catching a real mistake — the expo app numbers its rate-limiting and CSRF exceptions REQ-018 and REQ-019, not REQ-014 and REQ-015 like the other two, and the generated baseline had copied the wrong ids.

The mapping itself found seven things the prose security notes never said, because prose lists what an app does and rarely what it omits. Two are high risk: logout deletes the cookie but a self-contained token captured beforehand stays valid for the rest of its 8-hour life and re-authentication does not terminate the previous one (V7.2.4, V7.4.1, REQ-104), and seeded accounts whose passwords are published in this repository ship with every app because they are what the E2E suites sign in as (V6.3.2, REQ-106). The rest: no security headers of any kind and nothing clearing client state at session end (V3.2.1, V14.3.1, REQ-102), TLS and HSTS left to an edge the apps do not ship (REQ-101), no change-password function (REQ-105), a session cookie without the __Host- or __Secure- prefix (REQ-103), no documented remediation window for vulnerable dependencies (REQ-107), and for the two FastAPI apps an SPA fallback that joins the request path onto a filesystem path with no test proving traversal is rejected (REQ-108). The CSRF mitigation was also downgraded from mitigated to not-met, because nothing tests that a text/plain body is actually refused.

The user was asked before any of this was recorded, because an exception carries their name and these were new findings rather than transcriptions of risks they had already accepted, and chose to record all of them rather than fix them. Everything expires 2026-12-22.

The result is worth reading carefully: 30 met, 16 not applicable, 15 to 16 not met per app, on three apps that pass all 25 R3 controls and still do. The baseline did not make them worse; it made what was already true visible. security-controls and requirements-traceability now cite the two new artifacts from their readiness manifests instead of resting on prose alone.

Suite 263/263 (was 250). Kit 3.2.0, MINOR: a project without docs/evidence/security-baseline.json is not checked and no previously passing gate fails.

workItems.title: Supply-chain evidence: licenses, provenance and checksums
acceptance: Dependency licenses are collected as machine-readable evidence, not left implicit in the SBOM
Build provenance ties an artifact to the commit, workflow and runner that produced it
Published artifacts carry checksums a consumer can verify independently
workItems.notes:
Narrowed by the D-013 audit. The SBOM half is real: all three apps ship CycloneDX SBOMs and pinned lockfiles, and readiness.js requires the sbom control at R3. The other three things this row names do not exist anywhere — the words provenance, SLSA and license appear only in the roadmap itself (the other search hits are minified vendor bundles inside build output). EP-011 got close by materializing evidence/ci-run.json, which already records the workflow, run and commit that produced each verified build; turning that into real provenance plus checksums is a smaller job now than the original row implies.

Work done 2026-09-23. The design decision that carries the artifact is that the licence summary is DERIVED, never written: the validator reads the project's own SBOMs on every run, counts components per licence expression, and fails if the recorded numbers differ in either direction — undercounted, or naming a licence that appears in no SBOM. A hand-written licence inventory is a second copy of the SBOM that drifts from it, which is the contract-drift class EV-003 already named. The SBOMs are pinned by a sha256 the validator recomputes, so editing an SBOM invalidates the summary instead of silently changing what it describes; the error message names the ordinary cause, which is regenerating the SBOM and forgetting the digest, rather than implying an attack.

Licence expressions are recorded verbatim, including the broken ones. The three reference apps contain "MIT and ISC" (SPDX requires uppercase AND, so it does not parse), "MIT | MIT" (the publisher declares the same licence twice) and NONE. Normalising those away would hide that a publisher ships an unparseable licence field, so licenseOf() joins whatever is there and lets the malformed value be its own bucket. Every expression must then be answered: blanket-allowed by policy, reviewed individually with a note, or accepted-risk pointing at an approved exception from EP-002 — the same rule EP-003 uses, so accepted risk still has exactly one home per project.

Provenance is cross-checked rather than declared. repository, commit, workflow, runId and url must all match evidence/ci-run.json, the durable CI record EP-011 already materialises; a run whose conclusion is not success is refused outright; and the commit must be the revision the readiness manifest graded, because provenance pointing at a different build than the one declared passing is two documents describing two different pieces of software. Checksums are recomputed from the files on disk, never trusted as typed, and anything that genuinely has no digest — the container image, which the adopter builds from the Dockerfile and nobody pushes to a registry — goes in notPublished with a reason, because saying "there is none, and here is why" is better than letting a reader assume it was forgotten.

The first review found real things. One component in nextjs-postgres-crud and thirty in each FastAPI app resolve to no licence at all, which is not permissive but a grant that does not exist; recorded as REQ-201, low risk for one component and medium for thirty. One dependency is (BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0) and the record now states that this project takes the BSD option — without that, the dependency tree reads as containing GPL-2.0 code under obligation. Two conjunctive expressions carry an LGPL-3.0-or-later term, cleared on the stated basis that the components are unmodified and these apps are deployed rather than redistributed, with the condition written into the note that it must be revisited if an image is ever published.

Suite 277/277 (was 264). Kit 3.3.0, MINOR: a project without docs/evidence/supply-chain.json is not checked.

workItems.title: Operational readiness: backup, restore and incident hooks
acceptance: A restore is rehearsed and produces evidence, on the same footing as the migration-rollback rehearsal
Incident hooks are declared as a contract rather than described in a runbook paragraph
The operational controls cite that evidence instead of prose
verification: docker compose up -d db && node scripts/rehearse-backup-restore.mjs (in each reference app)
workItems.notes:
Narrowed by the D-013 audit. Health, logs and runbook are done and enforced: observability, health-check and runbook are required at R3, and every app ships a health endpoint, structured logging and docs/runbook.md. Backup and restore are mentioned in two of the three runbooks and in the db-migration rule, but nothing rehearses a restore and no evidence file records one, so the strongest operational claim in the model rests on a paragraph. The pattern to copy already exists in this repository — EP-006 rehearses migration rollback and writes machine-readable evidence — which is why this is narrow rather than open-ended.

Work done 2026-09-23. The audit's framing turned out to be half the story. standards/deployment-ready-contract.md's responsibility table says Buaflow delivers "migrations, rollback and backup/restore procedure" while the platform owns the production data window, and all three reference-app runbooks cited that same table to say "this repository has no automated backup step; that is an infrastructure/platform responsibility". That reads the table backwards: the procedure is ours, the schedule and retention and data policy are theirs. Collapsing the two is what left the strongest claim in the whole model — lose the data and you can get it back — resting on a paragraph nobody had to prove. All three runbooks now say what the contract says, and each gained a Backup and restore section with the real commands.

The rehearsal destroys things on purpose, because one that never destroys anything proves nothing. It fingerprints every row of every table (md5 of the ordered contents per table, combined into one sha256), takes a pg_dump -Fc and records the artifact's size and digest, runs DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE, verifies zero tables remain, restores with pg_restore, fingerprints again and requires an exact match. A restore that recreated empty tables would sail through a "do the tables exist" check and fails this one. It finishes by running the migration command the runbook's Recovery section tells an operator to run after a restore, confirming it is a no-op — an instruction that is only safe if it is. Everything runs through docker compose exec, so the rehearsal needs no Postgres client and no language environment of its own, unlike the existing migration-rollback rehearsals which shell out to python.

All three apps were really rehearsed in this session, against their own docker-compose Postgres, and all three came back identical. Nothing here is a transcript that was written rather than produced.

Incident hooks became a contract with five checkable parts: a signal specific enough to build an alert from, a detector whose files must exist, a severity, an owner that is a person rather than a team, and a firstResponse of the form file.md#anchor that the validator resolves against the real headings — a link to a heading somebody renamed fails at 2am otherwise, which is the worst possible time to find it. The anchor generator follows the rendered form including duplicate suffixes, and deliberately does not collapse runs of spaces: "web / backend" renders as "web--backend", and a collapsing version would be self-consistent here while producing links that 404 on the page where they are actually clicked. That was caught by a test expectation disagreeing with the implementation, and the implementation was the one that was wrong.

The completeness rule answers D-016's note instead of duplicating it: where a security baseline exists, every trust boundary it declares must be watched by at least one hook, and a hook naming a boundary that does not exist fails too. EP-005 therefore never restates a threat boundary — it makes the gap between knowing a boundary is there and knowing how you would find out it broke visible to a machine.

Suite 288/288 (was 277). Kit 3.4.0, MINOR.

workItems.title: Performance and accessibility budgets driven by the application profile
acceptance: Thresholds come from the application profile rather than being written per app
A profile that demands a stricter budget fails an app that only meets the looser one
The repeatable command and its threshold source are both recorded in the evidence
workItems.notes:
Narrowed by the D-013 audit. Measurement is done: performance and accessibility are required at R3, every app runs axe and a performance budget and ships the JSON evidence. What is missing is the word "profile-specific", which both the roadmap row and standards/deployment-ready-contract.md use. application-profile.schema.json carries controlOverride, architectureChoice and clarificationQuestion but no thresholds at all, so every budget today is a number chosen inside one app. That means a content site and a booking system are held to whatever each happened to pick, which is the opposite of what a profile contract is for.

Work done 2026-09-23. The split is the whole design: application-profile 1.1 holds the ceiling and why, and budget-evidence 1.0 holds what the app measured, the repeatable command that produced each number, and the file the number came out of. The evidence schema has no field for a threshold at all, deliberately — if it had one we would be back where we started, with an app setting its own exam and marking it. The old evidence literally read "budgetMs": 3000 next to a 47ms measurement, and nothing anywhere said where 3000 came from.

Measured numbers are re-derived from the cited evidence on every run, the same principle EP-004 applied to licence counts: timings are read by dot path out of the performance artifact, axeViolations is the length of the violations array and axeSeriousOrCritical counts the serious and critical impacts. Rounding is allowed, a different number is not. The metric vocabulary is closed, so a profile cannot set a ceiling on something no app measures, and the reverse is checked too: measuring a metric the profile does not budget is an error because it decides nothing. A budgeted metric nothing measures fails outright, because not measuring is not passing. A profile with no budgets at all is refused rather than treated as permissive, since a record citing it would look like a control while controlling nothing.

The behaviour EP-007 exists to produce is proven by test rather than by degrading a reference app: an app measuring 2200ms with two minor axe findings passes internal-crud and fails content on both axes, with identical measurements on both runs. The three real apps load in under 50ms with zero violations, so switching their profile would not have demonstrated anything.

Two smaller decisions worth keeping. The migrator moves a profile from 1.0 to 1.1 by raising the version and nothing else, and a test asserts it never invents budgets, because filling in defaults would be the kit deciding what somebody's application standards are. And internal-crud carries accessibility budgets even though the same profile marks the accessibility control not-applicable: if an app opts in, which all three reference apps did, that is the bar. axeSeriousOrCritical is 0 in all three shipped profiles, because a known internal audience is not a reason to ship a page a colleague cannot use at all.

The artifact-migration test had assumed every type's latest version was 1.0. It now reads the per-type latest, so the next minor bump fails loudly instead of quietly comparing against the wrong fixture.

workItems.title: Capability pack contract
acceptance: Superseded: one contract already covers both pack kinds
workItems.notes: Dropped by the D-013 audit as a duplicate, not as a change of mind. workItems.title: Model capability registry
acceptance: Dropped: the data would be stale faster than it could be maintained
workItems.notes: Dropped by the D-013 audit. A registry of context windows, tool-use support, cost and latency per model is a table that model vendors invalidate on their own schedule, often monthly, and this project has no mechanism and no reason to track it. Worse, it is the kind of artifact that is dangerous when slightly wrong: routing or capability decisions made from a stale registry fail quietly. The durable version of this need is MT-007 (work correctly when a capability is absent), which is kept, because it does not require knowing in advance which model has which feature.

workItems.title: Eval-driven model routing
acceptance: Dropped: routing without an eval harness and real tasks is guesswork with extra machinery
workItems.notes: Dropped by the D-013 audit, and this one can be reopened honestly later. Building routing first would mean choosing models from numbers produced by the three reference apps this repository wrote itself, which measures the apps, not the models. It also depended on MT-005, now dropped. acceptance: Dropped: there are no users to collect from

workItems.title: Internal opt-in usage capture across adopted projects
acceptance: A project is asked once, when Buaflow is started in it, whether to record usage; the answer is stored in the project and nothing is recorded, written or sent before a yes or after it is switched off

Lifecycle events are recorded without anyone typing them — intent opened, plan approved, /check result, verifier audit, /done merged — each carrying a schema version, the project, the task, the model that did the work and the kit version
Full content is kept (intent, spec, plan, acceptance criteria and check findings), because the owner accepts it for internal projects and the eval corpus is useless without it
Records from every opted-in project reach one private git repository; a failed sync never blocks, slows or fails a task, a commit or the gate — it waits and retries

From that repository alone, without opening any project: real intent/plan/AC can be turned into eval cases for the skills, /check outcomes can be compared by model, and every project's readiness and evidence freshness appear in one view
At least two internal projects other than this repository have opted in and produced records before this is called done
workItems.notes: Opened 2026-09-24 under D-028 as the fresh item EV-005 asked for once real adopters existed. The owner uses Buaflow internally on 2-5 projects through the plugin and wants their real work to feed Buaflow's development: reference cases, an eval corpus built from real intents and plans, a measure of how much the model changes AC coverage and rework, and one dashboard across projects. EV-009 already measured Bluepeak Hub by hand with ev-009-measurement-protocol.md; this item is that protocol recorded automatically on every opted-in project. Owner answers: internal only, confidentiality is not a concern, one-time consent per project, storage in a private git repository, all four benefits wanted from the first round. Open before spec: [NEEDS CLARIFICATION (data): what counts as rework — a /check that fails, a reopened task, or a follow-up fix task that points back — this decides which events must exist]. [NEEDS CLARIFICATION (architecture): does sync run from a hook at the end of a session or from buaflow ci/pre-push — decides whether it works for people who never push]. Default chosen, not asked: records are JSONL in the project until synced, one file per day. 2026-09-24: open questions resolved (rework = raw events for all three signals, definition in analysis; sync = local append, non-blocking sync at session start/end plus a manual command, never in the gate). Spec approved in three steps: 27 EARS acceptance criteria, design, and nine subtasks EV-011.1..9 tracked here. Progress: EV-011.1 done (usage.js core, usage-consent/usage-event 1.0 registered as internal because the feature is internal-only by R1 and a public type would force a release entry before EV-011.8; buaflow usage consent/status/record check; 20 tests). EV-011.1 closed 2026-09-24 after /check (no must-fix; owner approved) at commits 042d54b and b650bf9 on feat/EV-011-usage-capture — it merges with the single EV-011 PR. Carried into EV-011.4: usage status already tells people to run buaflow usage setup, which EV-011.4 adds; add a test there that every command a warning names actually parses. EV-011.2 implemented 2026-09-24, awaiting /check: hook usage-capture.js (SessionStart marker+reconcile+one-line notice, PostToolUse Write|Edit|MultiEdit on docs/intents|plans|backlog/tasks, PreToolUse Bash marker) wired in settings.json.tpl and the plugin; logic in usage.js handleHook. Decisions within the design: first contact records a baseline instead of replaying history, judging the file being written by its committed version; reconcile events carry data.source=reconcile so EV-011.5 can tell a pulled change from a session change; the commit is read from .git on disk because spawning git alone blew the 200 ms budget on Windows (post now ~40 ms including node start). SessionEnd is wired in EV-011.4 with sync. /check EV-011.2 round 1: /code-review found two must-fix — the root followed the session cwd after a cd (now the nearest .git above cwd, relative file_path resolved from cwd) and state.json was read-modify-written by every hook so a parallel Bash hook could overwrite seen (marker moved to marker.json, state written only by SessionStart and watched writes, both written via temp+rename); code-reviewer found none. Also dropped the unproven input.model object form. The timing test now budgets what the hook adds over a bare node start, because node start alone passed 150 ms under the loaded suite (flaked 1 in 3). workItems.title: Failure taxonomy
acceptance: A named, stable set of failure classes covers spec, implementation, integration, security, operations and tooling
Every class is grounded in a failure this repository actually hit, cited to where it happened, rather than invented from a category list
The taxonomy is machine-readable and validated, so a failure record cannot name a class that does not exist
workItems.notes: Chosen as the next item on 2026-09-23. Cheap because the data already exists and has been written down all session: a sync-hook data-loss race, a transitive advisory in a mobile dependency chain, a CI action requesting an SDK package Google removed, a regex that let a flag swallow a tool token, a pack asserting a file its app never had, a recipe installing two dependencies the real implementation avoids, and a verifier destroying the evidence it was verifying. Those are seven distinct classes observed in one repository, which is a better starting corpus than a taxonomy copied from a paper. Built 2026-09-23. Nine classes, each carrying an observedIn record with what happened, where, and what caught it: spec-gap, contract-drift, implementation-defect, integration-mismatch, supply-chain-finding, toolchain-failure, verification-gap, evidence-defect and guidance-defect. The grounding rule is enforced by a test rather than asked for in prose: every citation must resolve, so a work-item or decision id has to exist in state.json and a path has to exist on disk. A taxonomy that drifts into a copied category list fails the suite. The most useful field turned out to be detectedBy, required on every record with "nothing caught it" explicitly allowed, because that answer is what names an open gap. Reading it across the nine classes produces a work list from data rather than from guessing: contract-drift was caught by the pack binding check on its first run and implementation-defect by end-to-end tests that really failed, so those gates earn their keep, while spec-gap was caught only by a human reading a contract and evidence-defect only by git status after the damage was done, so those two are the holes. Deliberately NOT included: an operations-failure class. Nothing in this repository has ever run in production, so grounding one would require inventing an incident, which is exactly the failure this file exists to prevent. The hole is declared as a known gap with EV-009 named as what closes it, and a test asserts the class stays absent so nobody closes it on paper. The roadmap row asked for six categories (spec, implementation, integration, security, operations, tool); what the evidence actually supports is nine classes and one declared hole, which is a better answer than matching the original list. Ships as claude-setup/failure-taxonomy.js (catalog, record validation and a --list CLI), schemas/failure-record.schema.json with its template and registry entry, standards/failure-taxonomy.md, and 13 tests. A record naming a class that does not exist is rejected, which is what makes the taxonomy a contract rather than advice. Suite 182 to 195.

workItems.title: Compatibility and release policy for the kit itself
acceptance: The kit states what its own version number promises and what a major, minor and patch change mean for an adopter
A support matrix says which artifact schema versions each kit version reads
Deprecation has a stated path and a minimum notice, rather than being decided per change
workItems.notes: Chosen as the next item on 2026-09-23. BF-006 set a versioning and migration policy for artifacts and PP-010 exercised it for real by taking packs to 2.0 with a manual migration, but nothing covers the kit itself: package.json says 2.3.4 with no stated meaning, VERSION.md and UPGRADE.md exist without a policy behind them, and an adopter copying claude-setup/ into their project has no way to know what a Buaflow upgrade may break. The artifact policy is the model to follow, not to duplicate. Built 2026-09-23, and applied to the kit in the same change, because a policy that leaves the version number meaningless has not finished. The policy states one test for MAJOR, written from the adopter side rather than the author side: if the user has to do something, it is MAJOR, however small it looks from in here. By that test this release is 3.0.0, not 2.4.0 — pack went 1.0 to 2.0 with a manual migration, so any project holding .claude/packs/*.json must rewrite those files by hand. The support matrix is data rather than prose (schemas/compatibility.json), following principle 2, and scripts/check-compatibility.js makes it unable to lie: package.json must equal the newest release, every public artifact type in the registry must appear at its current version, a type in the matrix that the registry does not know is an error, releases must be newest-first and unique, and every MAJOR must both state what the adopter has to do and have a section in UPGRADE.md. It earned its place on the first run by reporting that package.json still said 2.3.4 while the matrix already declared 3.0.0. Deprecation policy: announce in a MINOR release first, 90 days minimum notice, a replacement is mandatory, and shortening the notice is allowed only with a note arguing for it — the checker rejects a short notice with no note, so a considered exception is distinguishable from an accident. The one exception on record is pack v1, announced and removed in the same release with no notice at all. That is recorded honestly with a note rather than backdated to look compliant, because the kit had no release policy when the change was made, which is the gap this item closes, and it is marked as the last change permitted to skip the step. The checker was refactored mid-build into a pure checkCompatibility function after a self-review found one of its own tests was a tautology that asserted a fact against itself and exercised nothing; the negative cases now feed the function directly. VERSION.md and UPGRADE.md gained v3.0.0 entries, including the warning that verifier.js --execute has side effects. Suite 195 to 211.

workItems.title: Change impact engine
acceptance: Changing an intent identifies the artifacts, contracts and tests that must be reviewed, from recorded links rather than from a guess
Impact is reported as a list a human or an agent can act on, not as a warning to read carefully
A link that cannot be resolved is reported as unknown impact, never as no impact
workItems.notes: Chosen as the next item on 2026-09-23. It scores highest on the model-durability test in D-011: the better the model, the more it changes per session and the less a human reads, so knowing what a change touches becomes more valuable rather than less. The links it needs largely exist — docs-lint already enforces the intent/spec/task chain, DV-002 extended traceability upstream to pain points, and readiness manifests tie controls to files and commands — so this is mostly making an existing graph queryable. The third acceptance criterion matters most: an unresolved link must read as unknown impact, because a change-impact tool that silently reports nothing is worse than none. Built 2026-09-23 on BC-004's graph. Impact travels in both directions, because changing a task affects the intent above it and not only what it points at; a one-directional walk would miss the thing most worth re-reading. Every affected artifact comes back with a specific action rather than a warning to read carefully, and with the path it was reached by, so the output is a list someone can work through. --depth bounds the blast radius for large graphs. The third acceptance criterion drove the design: an unresolved link inside the radius is reported as UNKNOWN impact and the CLI exits non-zero, so a script cannot read silence as safety. Three distinct cases are separated rather than flattened into "not found" — a node id that does not exist, a file that exists but that no artifact references (unknown, and it says so in those words), and a genuinely unaffected start. A start can be given as a file path as well as a node id, because what someone holds after editing is a filename, not a node id. Scores highest on the model-durability test from D-011: the better the model, the more it changes per session and the less a human reads, so knowing what a change touches gains value rather than losing it. 11 tests.

workItems.title: Convergence graph
acceptance: Requirement, design, data, API, UI, test and deployment artifacts are related in one machine-readable graph
A node with no path to a proof is reported, since an unconnected artifact is the shape most integration failures take
The graph is derived from artifacts that already exist, never maintained by hand
workItems.notes: Chosen as the next item on 2026-09-23. BC-005 already built a narrow slice of this — profile versus composed packs — and proved the approach works by reading two existing contracts rather than inventing a new one; PP-010 added a third edge by binding packs to the reference apps that implement them. This item generalizes that instead of starting over. It pairs with IC-006: the change-impact engine answers what a change touches, the convergence graph answers what is connected to nothing, and both read the same links. Built 2026-09-23 alongside IC-006, which reads the same graph. The graph is derived on every run from artifacts that already exist — intent and task frontmatter, pain-point ids cited in intent bodies, readiness controls and their evidence, packs and profiles and the controls they touch — so nobody maintains it by hand; a hand-maintained graph would be wrong inside a week. Two reports that are deliberately not merged: unconnected (no edges at all, in or out) and unproven (connected, but no path reaches a commit or an evidence node). Collapsing them would drown the real signal, because every not-yet-finished intent would read as an orphan and nobody would look at the list twice. Proof is reached in either direction on purpose: an intent counts as proven because a task points AT it and that task carries a commit, not because the intent points anywhere itself. A link whose target does not exist is recorded in unresolved and the target is never invented as a node, which is what IC-006 depends on — a silently dropped link becomes "no impact" later, the most dangerous answer a change-impact tool can give. This generalizes BC-005 rather than replacing it: that item proved the approach on one edge (profile versus composed packs) by reading two existing contracts instead of inventing a new one. All three reference apps come back fully connected with no unresolved links, asserted by a test. 11 tests.

workItems.title: Assumption/risk ledger with owner, impact, expiry and verification path
acceptance: Every guess a project builds on is recorded with a person who can confirm it, its impact, an expiry and how it will be checked
An open assumption past its expiry fails the gate; a refuted one must say what changed; the verifier, not the ledger, bounds the window
workItems.notes: Deliberately the same shape as EP-002 exceptions: an exception is a known gap someone accepted, an assumption is an unknown someone chose to proceed on. Owners like "AI" or "team" are refused because they cannot confirm anything. A manual confirmation (asking the business owner) is accepted as real evidence for an assumption, unlike for a requirement, but reported as not reproducible.

workItems.title: Smart clarification and a question budget
acceptance: A clarification question states which decision its answer changes (architecture, security, cost, data, scope, ux, legal); a question that changes none is not asked
More than eight open questions in one file is reported, pointing at defaults or assumptions instead
workItems.notes: Enforced as docs-lint warnings in 3.x so existing intents and specs do not fail on a MINOR upgrade. The trial's EV-002 eval run is the observed failure: four questions, only one with a recommendation.

workItems.title: Idea intake from issue trackers, CSV and plain lists
acceptance: GitHub and GitLab exports, a CSV with a title column and a plain bullet list become draft intents without inventing problem, evidence or outcome
The four /intent questions the source does not answer become tagged markers; nothing is imported twice or overwritten; the default is a dry run
workItems.notes: Interview and existing-docs intake stay with /intent and Phase A, which already take them as conversation; generator output is brownfield and goes through assess + Phase A. What was missing was batch import of work already waiting in another tracker, which Phase A.1 counted and then dropped.

workItems.title: Intent-to-requirement check: EARS acceptance criteria that trace to a test plan
acceptance: Every AC in docs/specs/*/requirements.md is one of the four EARS forms
Every AC id is referenced by design.md or tasks.md of the same spec
workItems.notes: The compiling is done by the AI in /spec (D-011: the AI of the day builds, Buaflow proves); this item is the proof half. Warnings in 3.x for the same upgrade reason as IC-002.

workItems.title: Feedback-to-change loop: evidence, proposal, eval, rollout or rollback
acceptance: Each change to the AI configuration records the evidence that motivated it and the eval cases it should decide
Rollout requires a clean baseline after-run of every expected case that passes at the current case revision, and no case that passed before failing after; rollback requires a reason
workItems.notes: Phase 8.1 already escalated lessons from AGENTS.md to rules to hooks; nothing recorded whether an escalation worked, and the trial's ablation found a hook whose removal changed nothing. Phase 8.4 still told readers to fill a Markdown results table that EV-004 removed; corrected here.

workItems.title: Reference app matrix
acceptance: The matrix records origin, surface and complexity of every project the kit is proven on, including the outside trial
Every in-repository app exists, an external one points at its record, and the unproven cells are printed on every check
workItems.notes: 4 of 12 cells proven. The empty cells are reported, not failed: principle 5 and D-011 chose depth over breadth and ruled out a fourth golden stack.

workItems.title: Graceful degradation: the workflow without tool-specific features
acceptance: The same core workflow renders as plain playbooks usable by a tool with no slash commands, subagents, inline commands, built-in reviewers, path-scoped rules or hooks, with a fallback for each feature a playbook uses
The guarantees that do not survive without session features are stated, and a feature core uses without a mapped fallback fails the check
workItems.notes: Not a vendor adapter (D-006): it is the floor every tool can fall to. Four guarantees are stated as session-only, including no-self-merge and protected files, because the gate cannot tell who edited a file.

workItems.title: Repair loop with limits
acceptance: A failing check is classified with the failure taxonomy before it is fixed, and each class has an attempt budget (environment and flaky failures: no code changes; spec gaps: none)
Stopping asks one question with the failing line, what was tried and the class, and a costly failure is recorded as a failure record
workItems.notes: Delivered as workflow content plus an eval case, because a repair loop is agent behaviour and the eval harness is how the kit checks behaviour. Grounded in K-9: the gate learned to name FLAKY in 3.7.0, but nothing told the agent that such a failure must not be fixed in code. The eval is unrun: this session wrote it and may not grade it.

workItems.title: Plugin manifest: Buaflow as a Claude Code plugin
acceptance: The session layer (skills, agents, guard hooks) installs as one Claude Code plugin generated from claude-setup/, with hooks running from ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}
Claude Code accepts the plugin in strict validation; what the plugin deliberately does not carry (gate, permissions, fitted rules) is stated
workItems.notes: Scoped to Claude Code by D-024. The roadmap row asked for a Buaflow-specific manifest (id/version/capability/permission/input/output/verification); Claude Code already has a plugin manifest and it is the one users install from, so inventing a second one for a single vendor would be surface without a consumer. Permissions stay in the project because Claude Code plugins cannot ship them.

workItems.title: Lockfile: which kit version and files a project installed
acceptance: buaflow lock --write records the kit version and the sha256 of every installed file copied from the kit
Without --write it reports each installed file as current, outdated, customized or drifted, and doctor reports the lock
workItems.notes: Grounded in the trial: its .claude/check-config.js was several releases old (the K-13 bug) and its guard-bash.js was changed on purpose, and nothing could tell those apart. There is no dependency resolver because the kit has no plugin dependencies to resolve; the row's resolver half has nothing to act on yet.

workItems.title: Permission model: audit what the project lets the AI do
acceptance: check-config fails a committed settings.json that allows every shell command or bypasses permissions
It warns when secrets (.env) are readable or WebFetch is unrestricted
workItems.notes: The permission model itself is Claude Code's; the kit's part is to make an unsafe committed configuration visible, the same way it makes an unsafe manifest visible.

workItems.title: MCP policy: every server is a recorded decision, pinned and without committed secrets
acceptance: Every .mcp.json server is explicitly enabled or disabled in settings, and blanket enableAllProjectMcpServers is reported
Secrets written into .mcp.json instead of ${VAR} references fail; npx/uvx packages without a pinned version are reported
workItems.notes: Only settings keys that are long established (enabledMcpjsonServers, disabledMcpjsonServers, enableAllProjectMcpServers) are relied on. Newer allow/deny-list keys for managed settings were reported by a documentation lookup but not verified here, so nothing depends on them.

workItems.title: Plugin conformance kit
acceptance: Any plugin directory is checked for a versioned manifest, hooks that stay inside the plugin and fetch nothing from the network, skills and agents with frontmatter, and no machine-specific paths
A deliberately broken plugin fails on each of those

workItems.title: Trust tiers from evidence, not from the publisher
acceptance: A plugin is local when it conforms and verified when every file also matches its checksum list and Claude Code validates it
A file edited after generation breaks its checksum and is caught
workItems.notes: No key signing: there is one publisher, and a signature nobody checks against a known key adds nothing a checksum in the same repository does not. Reopen when a second publisher exists.

workItems.title: Catalog v1
acceptance: A marketplace lists the Buaflow plugin with its version and passes strict validation
workItems.notes: One entry. The roadmap's own rule 9.4 says a catalog comes after contracts and conformance are stable; with one plugin and one trial the honest catalog is a single listing, not a discovery system.

workItems.title: Commercial capability packs
acceptance: Dropped by D-025: the building agent picks the provider and reads its current docs at task time; a kit pack would only be a stale copy
workItems.notes: Dropped by D-025 at the user's direction. What a pack would have added is the provider recipe, which is exactly what a current model plus a docs fetch at task time already does better and fresher. The part that is not the AI's job to remember — proving the result (webhook signature checked, idempotent payment handling, amounts computed on the server, PDPA consent and deletion) — is not domain-specific machinery; it belongs in the project's own requirements, security baseline (EP-003) and evals, which the kit already enforces.

workItems.title: Thailand packs
acceptance: Dropped by D-025: the building agent picks the provider and reads its current docs at task time; a kit pack would only be a stale copy
workItems.notes: Dropped by D-025 at the user's direction. What a pack would have added is the provider recipe, which is exactly what a current model plus a docs fetch at task time already does better and fresher. The part that is not the AI's job to remember — proving the result (webhook signature checked, idempotent payment handling, amounts computed on the server, PDPA consent and deletion) — is not domain-specific machinery; it belongs in the project's own requirements, security baseline (EP-003) and evals, which the kit already enforces.

workItems.title: Work isolation adapter
acceptance: Dropped by D-026: Claude Code isolates agents in worktrees natively
workItems.notes: Dropped by D-026. Claude Code already isolates parallel agents in their own git worktree (Agent isolation: "worktree", EnterWorktree). A kit adapter would wrap a feature the tool ships natively and track its changes.

workItems.title: Parallel scheduler
acceptance: Dropped by D-026: scheduling agents is the orchestrator's and model's job
workItems.notes: Dropped by D-026. Dependency ordering, concurrency and conflict avoidance between agents are planning, which is what the model and Claude Code's own orchestration improve at fastest. A kit scheduler would be the kind of machinery D-011 says the AI should own; Buaflow keeps the part it owns — proving the merged result.

workItems.title: Plugin-first adoption: the whole kit ships in the plugin
acceptance: A project can adopt Buaflow with the plugin alone: no buaflow/ folder is cloned, and START-HERE, the phases and the CLI are read and run from the plugin
The project-side controls (gate, checkers, control sets, seeds) are installed by one command that never overwrites a file the team changed
A project whose session layer comes from the plugin passes check-config, and doctor warns when the plugin is enabled but nothing guards a push outside the session
verification: claude plugin install buaflow@buaflow into a throwaway CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, then run the cached kit-context hook and the cached CLI install
workItems.notes: Opened from the user's question on 2026-09-24: why install the plugin and still clone the folder. 3.11 plugin carried only skills/agents/hooks; everything the phases read and the CLI lived in the folder. The plugin now carries kit/ (192 files, ~1.7 MB; reference-apps, manual, core and the kit tests left out) and a SessionStart hook that states the kit path, because the Claude Code docs guarantee ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} substitution in hook commands but not in skill text. The plugin cache is plain files with no .git, so install detects an old kit file through the lock it writes rather than kit history. Verified by a real install into a throwaway config: the cache held kit/, the hook reported the cached path, and the cached CLI installed a project. What the plugin still cannot do, and the docs say so: install itself for teammates (the marketplace is added from project settings, the plugin is not), and carry permissions, rules or stack.json.

decisions.decision: Evolve Buaflow as a model-agnostic application production system, not merge the reviewed AI-DLC starter.
decisions.reason: Buaflow's advantage is enforceable production qualification and portable handoff; the reviewed starter contributes patterns, not a compatible product core.
decisions.impact: Adopt decision records, adapters, traceability and teaching examples selectively while retaining Buaflow's lifecycle and gates.

decisions.decision: Target R3 Production Candidate rather than hosting or deploying applications for users.
decisions.reason: This preserves portability and keeps Buaflow focused on turning intent into verifiable deployable artifacts.
decisions.impact: Deployment rehearsal and manifests are in scope; operating a hosted control plane is not currently in scope.

decisions.decision: Use machine-readable state as canonical and Markdown as the explanatory view.
decisions.reason: Markdown-only completion states drift and cannot reliably drive gates or cross-model handoff.
decisions.impact: New core artifacts require schemas, validators and migration rules.

decisions.decision: Close M2 by (1) scoping EP-001 as a schema + generator script (not schema-only, not provenance/checksums) and (2) satisfying M2's 'convergence checks' criterion with a narrow profile-vs-pack contradiction check inside PP-007's pack-composition.js, tracked as a scoped-down BC-005, instead of waiting on BC-001..004.
decisions.reason: The user asked to jointly decide M2 scope before continuing (2026-09-23). For EP-001, a generator was chosen over a bare schema because a format nobody can produce isn't 'ครบ' (complete) in practice; provenance/checksums were excluded because that is EP-004's named scope and duplicating it there would blur the two. For convergence checks, full BC-005 (schema/API/migration/UI/requirement drift) needs BC-001..004 (agent I/O contract, work isolation, scheduler, convergence graph) which don't exist yet and would be a large, premature ecosystem surface to build just to close M2; PP-007 already noted its pack-composition.js as 'a small step toward M2's convergence checks, not the whole of it', so extending that same tool to catch one real, concrete contradiction (a profile declaring a control not-applicable while a chosen pack proves that exact control) was the smallest true instance of a 'convergence check' available without new machinery.
decisions.impact: M2 ('Repeatable Web Production': two web stacks, core capability packs, convergence checks, evidence bundle) is now fully done. The full BC-005 vision (schema/API/migration/UI/requirement drift detection across BC-001..004) remains open and unscoped; do not treat this BC-005 entry as having satisfied it. current.milestone moves to M3.

decisions.decision: Reviewed an external research document, 'Buaflow: AI-Native SDLC + Agentic Engineering,' written by the user's friend. Added a new 'Discovery and Validation' workstream (DV-001..003) to BUAFLOW_PRODUCT_ROADMAP.md, positioned before Intent Compiler, and pulled DV-001..003 into state.json as backlog. Did not create a separate workstream for the research's proposed Agentic Engineering layer (Orchestrator, Agent Contract, autonomy tiers A0-A4, agent run records) because it substantially overlaps with the already-planned BC-001..007 workstream at M3; added a pointer note after the BC-* table instead so that detail is not lost.
decisions.reason: Comparing the research against the current roadmap and phase docs found two gaps nothing existing covers: no evidence/pain-point/as-is/to-be discovery layer upstream of the Intent Compiler (Phase 1 is requirement Q&A, Phase A is technical inventory only, neither captures pain-point evidence or root cause), and Phase 8's feedback loop is config-learning only, not post-release business-outcome measurement. Everything else the research proposed (Orchestrator, Agent Contract, execution isolation, independent verification) already has a home in BC-001..007. Refusing manual-only proof was the rule with the most teeth, and the repository supplied its own justification: nextjs-postgres-crud's traceability table claimed the audit trail was proven by observing rows in a live database during PP-003, which is evidence stored in a session that no longer exists. The forever loophole is closed in EP-010's own shape — --max-window-days, unset means reported not judged, 90 days in npm run check for the reference apps. gate.js supplies no window on purpose, because an internal tool and a bank reach different answers about an identical exception. The unlicensed components are a real obligation rather than a formatting complaint — thirty per FastAPI app, because the SBOM generator resolves nothing for Python distributions that declare their licence only in free-text classifiers, which makes improving that generator a concrete piece of future work rather than a vague wish. The dual-licensed dependency now records which option this project takes, and any future baseline that omits that choice will read as carrying a GPL obligation it does not have. And the LGPL clearances are conditional in writing: they hold because these apps are deployed rather than redistributed, so publishing an image would require revisiting them. The provenance cross-check also gives EP-011's evidence/ci-run.json a second consumer, which makes it harder to let that file go stale unnoticed.

decisions.decision: Closed EP-005 with an operational-readiness artifact and a backup/restore rehearsal that really drops the schema. The rehearsal fingerprints every row before and after and requires an exact match, and the validator reads the transcript rather than trusting a reference to it: ok must be true, the data must have come back identical, and the digest is recomputed. Incident hooks became a contract with a signal, a detector whose files exist, a severity, a named owner and a runbook anchor resolved against real headings; where a security baseline exists, every trust boundary it declares must be watched. Also corrected all three runbooks, which had been citing the delivery contract's responsibility table to disclaim a responsibility that table assigns to Buaflow. Kit 3.4.0, MINOR.
decisions.reason: The D-013 audit said nothing rehearses a restore and no evidence file records one, which was true, but the reason was a misread contract rather than an oversight: standards/deployment-ready-contract.md assigns the backup/restore PROCEDURE to Buaflow and the production data window to the platform, and the runbooks cited that table while claiming the whole subject was someone else's. Once the procedure is ours, it has to be rehearsed like the migration rollback is, and the rehearsal has to destroy something or it proves nothing. Comparing a content fingerprint rather than a table list is what makes it a data test: the failure mode worth catching is a restore that brings the schema back and not the rows. Requiring incident hooks to resolve to a real runbook heading follows the same reasoning as every other check added this week — the instruction that is wrong is the one nobody reads until the night it matters.
decisions.impact: Three things carry forward. The rehearsal is Docker-only by design, which makes it the first rehearsal in this repository that an adopter can run without matching the app's language environment, and the two migration-rollback rehearsals that shell out to python are now the odd ones out. The boundary-coverage rule ties EP-005 to EP-003 rather than duplicating it, so adding a trust boundary later fails the gate until someone says how its failure would be detected — which is the intended cost. And the anchor checker is reusable: any future artifact that points at a runbook section can use headingAnchors() instead of inventing a second, subtly different slug rule. The rehearsals were run against a standalone Postgres on a spare port because the machine already had an unrelated stack on 5432; the committed scripts default to docker compose and take BACKUP_REHEARSAL_CONTAINER only as an override.

decisions.decision: Closed EP-007 by splitting the budget in two: application-profile 1.1 declares the ceiling and its reasoning, and a new budget-evidence 1.0 artifact records what the app measured, with the command and the source file for each number and no field for a threshold. Measured values are re-derived from the cited evidence, an unmeasured budgeted metric fails, and a profile with no budgets is refused. The migrator raises a profile from 1.0 to 1.1 without inventing budgets. Kit 3.5.0, MINOR. M4 is complete.
decisions.reason: The D-013 audit found that measurement was done and enforced at R3 while the word profile-specific, used by both the roadmap and standards/deployment-ready-contract.md, had no implementation: application-profile.schema.json carried no thresholds, so every budget was a number one app chose for itself. The shipped evidence made it plain, with budgetMs 3000 sitting next to a 47ms result and nothing saying where 3000 came from. Putting the ceiling in the profile is what makes a content site and an internal tool different in a way a machine can act on, and leaving the ceiling out of the evidence artifact is what stops the split from collapsing back. Re-deriving the measured numbers follows EP-004: a figure typed by hand is a figure that can be optimistic.
decisions.impact: Changing one line — the profile id in an app's budget record — now changes what that app must meet, with no code change, which is what profile-specific was always supposed to mean. Three consequences. The metric vocabulary is closed at four entries, so extending it is a deliberate schema change rather than a free-text field that quietly diverges per project. The migrator's refusal to invent budgets means every adopter on a 1.0 profile has to choose their own thresholds, which is slower and correct. And application-profile is the first artifact in this repository to take a minor version, which exposed that the migration test assumed 1.0 was universal; that test now follows the registry. Still deferred and worth its own item: the application profiles live in claude-setup/tests/fixtures/profiles, which is exactly the situation D-012 fixed for packs — a product catalogue under a test-fixture path — and EP-007 has just made them load-bearing at runtime for the first time. It was left alone here because moving them touches fourteen files including comments in reference-app source, which is a change the user should decide on rather than one folded into a budget item.

decisions.decision: Registered EV-002, EV-004 and EV-008 as work items in development/state.json, and started EV-004 first. M5's completion criteria in BUAFLOW_PRODUCT_ROADMAP.md section 7 name four items — EV-009, EV-004, EV-002, EV-008 — and state.json contained only EV-009. The other three existed solely as rows in the section 6 workstream table, which scripts/check-roadmap.js does not read.
decisions.reason: A milestone whose criteria are invisible to the checker is the same failure this product was built to stop: a status that is true because it is written down rather than because it was derived. Reading state.json alone gave 'M5 has one item left', which is wrong by three. EV-004 goes first because EV-002 needs something to score against, and because EV-009 just demonstrated the gap it closes — five eval cases prepared for a real outside project were deliberately left unrun, since the session that wrote the config could not credibly grade it, and no part of the current Markdown eval format can record or enforce that.
decisions.impact: M5 now shows four tracked items instead of one. current.focus holds EV-009 and EV-004, which is the WIP limit of 2, so no third item can start until one of them closes. EV-008 depends on EV-009 on purpose, so onboarding cannot be written before the first outside trial has said where readers get stuck.

decisions.decision: Closed EV-004 by splitting the eval format in two — eval-case 1.0 holds the question, eval-run 1.0 holds one judgement of it — and by making a run name the exact case revision it judged. The score is re-derived from the per-criterion verdicts on every read, a run graded by the case's own author is refused, and a run that continued an earlier session cannot pass. The four Markdown starter cases were converted and the Markdown format was removed rather than kept alongside.
decisions.reason: The old format's results table could not say which revision of a case a row had judged, so editing a case to be easier left every earlier "ผ่าน" in place, still reading as a pass. That is the same class of defect the whole kit exists to remove: a status that is true because it was written down. Keeping both formats would have meant two ways to record the same claim, only one of which could be checked, so the Markdown one went. The refusal to let a case's author grade it comes from EV-009, where five cases were prepared for a real outside project and deliberately left unrun for exactly that reason — a constraint the old format had no way to record.
decisions.impact: Kit 3.6.0 (MINOR): additive, because a project with no docs/evals/*.json is not checked and no previously-passing gate starts failing. Projects with Markdown cases convert by hand — no migrator exists, because converting would mean inventing the criterion ids the format rests on, and UPGRADE.md says so rather than guessing. npm run check now validates the kit's own four cases against this repository's tree, so a case cannot outlive the rule it tests. M5 drops to three open items: EV-002, EV-008 and EV-009, and current.focus returns to EV-009 alone.

decisions.decision: Ran EV-009's deliberately-unrun eval baseline by splitting authoring, answering and grading into three separate sessions, closed EV-002, and marked EV-009 blocked rather than done.
decisions.reason: The baseline was left unrun because the session that wrote the configuration would have graded itself. A fresh claude -p per case in a disposable, remote-less clone with the cases removed answers, and a second fresh claude -p that sees only the case and the transcript grades; the eval-run format records gradedBy and the harness refuses self-grading, so the separation is checkable rather than asserted. EV-009 cannot be done: reviewer-minutes need a human reviewer and the R1->R2 leg needs a CI run blocked on billing, and the acceptance asks for measured numbers, not narrated ones. Blocked with a reason is the honest status and frees the WIP slot.
decisions.impact: The trial project now has ten valid eval runs and a benchmark score (0.39) computed by the same command that scores the reference apps (0.97). Four new findings (K-11..K-14) and the EV-004 failure feed the kit. Anyone can unblock EV-009 by following development/trials/ev-009-measurement-protocol.md; no code is waiting on it.

decisions.decision: EV-008 (onboarding) now depends on EV-010 instead of EV-009.
decisions.reason: D-020 made EV-008 wait on EV-009 so onboarding would be written from what an outside adoption actually got wrong rather than imagined problems. That material now exists (K-1..K-14, the eval baseline) and the fixable parts are fixed in EV-010 and kit 3.8.0. The part of EV-009 still open, reviewer-minutes and a CI run, carries no information about where a reader gets stuck, so waiting on it would delay onboarding without improving it.
decisions.impact: EV-008 becomes startable. Its acceptance is unchanged: troubleshooting must still come from the recorded findings and every command it names must exist.

decisions.decision: Following the user's instructions of 2026-09-23 (evening): (1) reviewer-minutes for EV-009 are measured by an AI-proxy reviewer — a separate fresh session reviewing a separate builder session — with the risk that it is not human time explicitly accepted by the user; (2) hosted CI is replaced by a local clean-checkout run (buaflow ci) until a project goes live with free CI, and that closes the R1->R2 leg; (3) which paths are locked (K-14) is decided per project, and the kit only requires rules and protected paths to agree; (4) the no-self-merge rule stays where it is for now; (5) after M5, M6 is scoped to Claude Code only (no Codex/Copilot adapters) plus plugin/MCP, and the unscheduled roadmap items (IC-002..005, EV-006, EV-001, MT-007, BC-007) are pulled into M6.
decisions.reason: The user said so directly, and each choice is consistent with earlier decisions: D-006/D-008 already limited adapters to Claude until asked; D-011 already said Buaflow proves and the AI builds, which is how IC-002..005 and EV-006 were built (validators and warnings, not generators); the AI-proxy reviewer keeps the separation EV-004 made enforceable (builder and reviewer are different sessions) even though it cannot be a human.
decisions.impact: EV-009 can close with its four numbers, one of them labelled as an AI proxy wherever it is reported. Items that D-011 deliberately parked stay parked and are not reopened by (5): BC-001/002/003 (parallel scheduling) and PP-008/009 (commercial and Thai packs, which D-011 and D-014 say may only exist as recipe-and-assertion packs proven by a real implementation — no project in hand needs one). MT-003/004 stay unstarted.

decisions.decision: PP-008 and PP-009 are dropped and M7 (Domain Advantage) is closed without work. MT-006 is recorded as dropped everywhere. The next milestone is M8 (parallel build, BC-001..003), still awaiting the user's confirmation of scope.
decisions.reason: The user pointed out that when an app needs payment, PDPA or LINE, the building agent already chooses the tool and fetches its current documentation during the task, and models keep getting better at it, so a pack proven in advance adds a stale copy rather than knowledge. D-011 (the AI builds, Buaflow proves) supports this: the proof side — signature checks, idempotency, consent and deletion — is generic and already lives in requirements, the security baseline and evals. MT-006 was inconsistent between state.json (dropped by D-013) and the roadmap's parked table. The user also runs several agents in parallel, which is the reopen condition written for BC-001..003.
decisions.impact: The catalog stays at the packs that are already proven. current.focus moves from M7 (which has no items left) to BC-001 under M8, status backlog; nothing starts until the user confirms the scope.

decisions.decision: BC-001, BC-002 and BC-003 are dropped and M8 (Parallel Build) closes without work. With nothing left open, current.focus is empty and current.milestone stays at M6, the last milestone that closed with work; check-roadmap.js now allows an empty focus only when no item is open.
decisions.reason: The user asked whether a much stronger Claude Code would handle parallel agents by itself, and to drop the items if so. It largely does already: worktree isolation is native, and subagents, workflows and agent teams split and schedule work — planning is where models improve fastest. Under D-011 the AI builds and Buaflow proves, and the proof for parallel work already exists: the pre-push gate and buaflow ci verify the merged result from a clean checkout. The same reasoning dropped PP-008/009 in D-025.
decisions.impact: The roadmap has no open work items. MT-003/004 remain parked until the user asks. New work starts as a fresh item written from a real need (a failure seen in a real project, or a user request), not from this plan.

decisions.decision: Buaflow is adopted plugin-first (PE-008, kit 3.12.0): the plugin carries the whole kit and /buaflow:start, and buaflow install writes what must live in the project. The buaflow/ folder route stays supported.
decisions.reason: The user asked why the plugin still needed the folder, and whether the parts a plugin cannot carry reduce effectiveness. They do not when they are written into the project in Phase 7, which is what install does deterministically; they do when a project stops at the plugin, which doctor and check-config now report. Same D-011 line: Claude Code owns installation of the session layer, Buaflow keeps the gate that runs without it.
decisions.impact: README, QUICKSTART, UPGRADE, START-HERE, Phase 6/7 and CLI.md lead with the plugin. The UPGRADE fast path is two commands. Milestone M9 holds PE-008 and is complete.

decisions.decision: Reopen usage capture as a new item, EV-011, rather than reviving EV-005, scoped to internal projects the owner runs with one-time consent per project and a private git repository as the store.
decisions.reason: D-013 dropped EV-005 because the only source was this repository measuring itself, and wrote the reopening condition down: real adopters, and an item written against their needs. Both now hold. EV-009 closed today on Bluepeak Hub, and the owner reports 2-5 internal projects using Buaflow through the plugin (PE-008). The privacy concern that made D-013 wary of building a collection path first does not apply: the projects are the owner's, the owner accepts full content, and consent is still asked once per project.
decisions.impact: EV-011 sits in M5 as backlog awaiting the owner's go-ahead to spec. EV-005 stays dropped with its reason, so the history of why it was not built is kept. If EV-011 produces enough real eval runs to compare models, MT-006 (model routing) meets its own reopening condition and should be written as a new item from that data. current moves from the completed M9 to M5 with EV-011 in focus.
